strengths: Novel and well-motivated combination of order-invariant/permutation-based autoregressive generative modeling with GRPO-style policy-gradient training for discrete EDAs, replacing the NP-hard structure-learning step of classical multivariate EDAs (e.g., BOA, MIMIC) with a single continuous optimization problem.

Extensive theoretical grounding: rigorous derivations connecting the proposed objective to PPO/TRPO policy-gradient theory (Appendix B-C), to Information-Geometric Optimization / natural gradient (Appendix G), and an insightful interpretation of random-order training as information-preserving structural dropout with residual/hierarchical structuring effects (Appendix E), including a convergence analysis under infinite data/capacity (Appendix D).

Very large-scale and carefully designed empirical evaluation, benchmarking against essentially the entire Nevergrad library (500+ algorithms), three classical EDAs (PBIL, MIMIC, BOA), and Tabu search, across three NP-hard problem families (QUBO, NK, NK3) at three sizes, with statistical significance testing (t-tests) supporting the reported rankings.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of random generation vs. training orders, comparisons with naive input-dropout alternatives, sensitivity analyses on population size, KL penalty coefficient, and network depth, plus an interesting gray-box experiment using a known interaction graph.

The method shows a clear, favorable scaling trend with instance size (best or near-best on n=128/256 while less competitive at n=64), suggesting the approach could be practically relevant for larger combinatorial instances where classical structure learning becomes prohibitive.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is currently unmet: the reproducibility statement explicitly says code 'will be published soon,' meaning no verifiable implementation accompanies the submission despite the paper's heavy reliance on many implementation-level details (masking schemes, clipping thresholds, optimizer settings) that would be hard to reproduce from the text alone.

The comparison protocol conflates function-evaluation budgets (10,000 calls for the proposed method) with wall-clock time budgets (one hour) for Nevergrad baselines; given the reported per-instance runtime of the RL-EDA (minutes on GPU/CPU), it is unclear whether the head-to-head comparisons are compute-matched, which could bias comparisons in the paper's favor for equal-evaluation-count criteria while ignoring substantially higher per-evaluation training cost.

The proposed method underperforms on the smallest instances (n=64) and fails to converge within budget on the most rugged landscapes (NK3, K=8), which is an important limitation for the paper's overarching claim of consistently avoiding catastrophic failures and performing robustly 'without requiring any change to its hyperparameters.'

No empirical comparison to the directly inspirational permutation-invariant autoregressive baseline (σ-GPT) or other modern neural order-agnostic generators mentioned in related work, leaving the specific advantage of the proposed architecture/training scheme over closely related neural approaches somewhat unaddressed empirically.

The architecture uses per-variable parameter sets (θ ∈ R^{n×m}), and while the paper acknowledges parameter sharing as future work for scaling, no experiments test scalability beyond n=256, limiting confidence in claims about applicability to substantially larger combinatorial problems.

The paper's presentation defers almost all quantitative results, ablations, and many methodological justifications to a very extensive appendix (14 sections), leaving the main text comparatively thin on interpretable takeaways; core empirical claims (e.g., 'frequently achieves the best performance') rely heavily on appendix tables not fully summarized in the body.

Evaluation is restricted to synthetic benchmark problems (QUBO, NK, NK3); no real-world or structured combinatorial applications are used to validate practical usefulness beyond controlled synthetic landscapes.

strengths: The paper provides an unusually thorough experimental validation, benchmarking against roughly 500 algorithms from Nevergrad plus classical EDAs (PBIL, MIMIC, BOA) and Tabu search, across three NP-hard problem families (QUBO, NK, NK3) and three problem sizes, with statistical significance testing.

The theoretical derivation connecting the proposed order-invariant PPO/GRPO objective to policy-gradient theory, PPO-KL surrogate objectives, and the Information-Geometric Optimization framework is carefully worked out in the appendices, giving the method a principled grounding.

The interpretation of random-order training as an information-preserving structural dropout (as opposed to naive input dropout, which is shown both theoretically and empirically to be less effective) is a genuinely interesting and non-trivial insight.

Extensive ablation studies are provided (structural dropout variants, known vs. unknown interaction graphs, population size, KL penalty coefficient, network depth), which help isolate which components of the method actually contribute to its performance.

The method is simple to implement (MLP-based per-variable heads with causal masking) and does not require learning explicit dependency graphs, avoiding the NP-hard structure-learning step of classical multivariate EDAs like BOA.
weaknesses: No code has been released at submission time ("source code ... will be published soon"), which is a significant reproducibility concern for a paper whose central claims rest on many specific implementation details (masking schemes, order sampling, hyperparameters) and comparisons against hundreds of external baselines.

Evaluation is restricted entirely to synthetic benchmark problems (QUBO, NK, NK3); there is no validation on any real-world or application-driven combinatorial optimization task, which limits the practical significance of the claimed improvements.

The method's performance is inconsistent: it is not competitive on the smallest instances (n=64), and it explicitly fails to converge within budget on the most rugged NK3 landscapes (K=8), which is an important limitation that is acknowledged but not resolved.

The large-scale comparison against 500+ Nevergrad algorithms, while impressive in scope, is presented mainly as per-instance-type rankings/win counts rather than an aggregated, holistic statistic (e.g., overall average rank or win-rate across the full grid of instances), making it harder to assess overall relative performance robustly.

Fairness of the comparison is unclear: the proposed method uses GPU-accelerated batched training with a fixed wall-clock budget different from the 1-hour-per-instance budget given to Nevergrad baselines (which are typically CPU-only), so it is not obvious the comparison is normalized on equal computational grounds.

The technical novelty is an incremental combination of existing ideas (permutation-invariant/NADE-style autoregressive modeling, σ-GPT-style order sampling, dropout-as-regularization, GRPO/PPO-KL, IGO advantage normalization) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism, and the paper does not compare against other modern neural approaches to combinatorial black-box optimization (e.g., GFlowNets or other neural EDA variants) beyond Nevergrad and classical EDAs.

Key hyperparameters (population size λ=10, KL coefficient β=1, network architecture) are fixed across very different problem types, and while sensitivity analyses are provided, the paper does not offer principled guidance on how a practitioner should select them for a new, unseen problem class.

The presentation is dense and contains minor errors/typos (e.g., 'solide lines', 'dentified'), and the paper relies heavily on appendices (over 25 pages) to carry much of the technical and empirical substance, making the main text feel somewhat incomplete on its own.

strengths: The paper proposes a genuinely novel synthesis of ideas: casting discrete multivariate EDAs as an autoregressive generative process trained with random variable orderings, combined with a GRPO-style policy-gradient update. This sidesteps the NP-hard structure-learning step required by classical multivariate EDAs (MIMIC, BOA) while retaining the ability to model complex inter-variable dependencies.

Substantial theoretical backing: the paper carefully derives the PPO/GRPO surrogate objective for both fixed and randomly permuted generation/training orders (Appendices B, C), proves that the Monte-Carlo GRPO objective is an unbiased estimator of a well-defined population objective (Appendix D), connects the framework to Information-Geometric Optimization and natural gradient descent (Appendix G), and offers an insightful theoretical interpretation of order-permutation training as information-preserving structured dropout, including a quantitative comparison to standard input dropout (Appendix E).

Extremely thorough empirical evaluation, benchmarking against essentially the entire Nevergrad library (500+ algorithms) plus classical EDAs (PBIL, MIMIC, BOA) and Tabu search, across three NP-hard problem families (QUBO, NK, NK3) at three sizes, with 100 independent runs per configuration.

Extensive and well-designed ablation studies isolating the contribution of each design choice: comparison of the four order-sampling variants, structural dropout vs. permutation-invariance, use of known vs. unknown interaction graphs, sensitivity to population size, KL penalty coefficient, and network depth — this level of ablation is uncommon and strengthens the soundness of the causal claims made about the method's components.

Honest discussion of limitations, including failure to converge on the most rugged NK3 instances (K=8) and the tradeoffs of larger/smaller population and KL coefficients, rather than only presenting favorable results.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is currently unsupported: the reproducibility statement explicitly says code 'will be published soon,' meaning at the time of review no code is available, which is a nontrivial concern given the complexity of the training pipeline (custom masking, GRPO with order resampling, etc.).

Scalability evidence is limited to n ≤ 256; the architecture uses a separate parameter set per output dimension (θ ∈ R^{n×m}), and while the authors mention parameter sharing as a possible extension, no experiments demonstrate behavior at larger, more realistic problem sizes (thousands of variables), leaving scalability claims speculative.

The abstract's claim that the method 'consistently avoids catastrophic failures' is in tension with the reported non-convergence on NK3 K=8 instances (Appendix M.6, Figure 13b) and the comparatively mediocre performance on n=64 instances (Table 3), suggesting the claim is somewhat overstated relative to the presented evidence.

The main comparison table involves 500+ algorithms with pairwise significance tests using a fixed p-value threshold (0.001) without correction for multiple comparisons, which could inflate the apparent number of statistically significant wins/losses.

There is a methodological asymmetry in the experimental protocol: Nevergrad competitors were run under a one-hour wall-clock budget while the proposed method and comparisons are reported vs. number of function evaluations; since different algorithms have very different per-evaluation overhead, it is unclear whether all baselines were given a fair chance to exhaust their allotted evaluation budget within the time limit.

The paper only evaluates synthetic benchmark problems (QUBO, NK, NK3); there is no application to a real-world or structured combinatorial task, which would help substantiate the practical significance of the proposed order-invariant approach beyond controlled synthetic landscapes.

The Learned-σ-RL-EDA variant, which attempts to learn generation order via a Plackett-Luce distribution, underperforms and fails to converge within budget — while this supports the paper's central claim (that explicit structure learning is unnecessary), it also suggests fragility in one of the paper's own proposed extensions that is not deeply diagnosed.

strengths: The paper provides a rigorous theoretical derivation connecting order-invariant autoregressive generative models, PPO/GRPO-style policy optimization, and the classical EDA/IGO framework, including convergence analysis in the infinite-data/infinite-capacity regime and an explicit link to natural gradient descent (Appendix G).

Extensive and carefully designed empirical evaluation: three NP-hard problem families (QUBO, NK, NK3) at multiple sizes, 10 instances per configuration, 100 independent runs per algorithm/instance-distribution, and comparison against >500 Nevergrad algorithms plus classical EDAs (PBIL, MIMIC, BOA), with statistical significance testing.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of random generation/training orders versus naive structural dropout, known interaction graphs, population size, KL coefficient, network depth, and number of training epochs, which convincingly show that the double random-order mechanism is not simply reducible to input dropout.
Validation on a real-world benchmark (NAS-Bench-101) in addition to synthetic benchmarks, and a scalability study (parameter-sharing variant) showing feasibility on instances of size 1024.
Good reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, computational complexity analysis, wall-clock times, and stated availability of code/instances in supplementary material.

Honest discussion of limitations, e.g., slower early-budget convergence and rugged landscape failure cases, followed by a principled curriculum-based fix (dropout annealing) rather than hiding weaknesses.
weaknesses: Core novelty is an incremental combination of existing ideas (order-agnostic autoregressive generation à la σ-GPT/NADE, GRPO-style rank-based advantages, PPO-KL regularization); the conceptual leap beyond prior order-invariant autoregressive modeling and EDA-as-RL framings is modest.

The architecture requires one small MLP per variable (O(n) networks, O(n^2 h) parameters), which scales poorly; the paper's own results show the method fails on n=1024 without a separate parameter-sharing variant, and even then requires substantially different hyperparameters/architecture, raising questions about a single unified recipe.

Performance is inconsistent across regimes: the method is not competitive at small budgets (1,000 evaluations) or small instance sizes (n=64) without ad hoc curriculum adaptations (ρ parameter, Appendix P), and it fails to converge within budget on the most rugged NK3 (K=8) landscapes, undermining the claim of hyperparameter-free robustness advertised in the main text.

The comparison against 500+ Nevergrad algorithms, while impressively broad, includes many algorithms not designed for the discrete setting (continuous PSO/CMA-ES variants), and the ranking-based presentation in the main paper is somewhat selective (only two example instance types shown in the main text), pushing most substantive quantitative results into a very large appendix, which reduces the self-containedness and clarity of the main paper.

Several theoretical claims (e.g., dropout-as-regularization arguments in Appendix E/F, residual-structuring argument) are heuristic/informal rather than rigorously proven, despite being presented with substantial mathematical notation that may overstate their rigor.

No comparison to other neural EDA or RL-based combinatorial construction approaches beyond Nevergrad and classical EDAs (e.g., no comparison to modern neural combinatorial optimization construction heuristics using attention/Transformer architectures, despite the paper explicitly positioning itself relative to such methods in Section 1).
